blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Preventing overselling

rows: Read status, then write if available
Incorrect under concurrency: the check and the write are separate
`UPDATE ... WHERE status =` `'AVAILABLE'`; success = one row changed
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, then check and update
Holds locks while the transaction runs; deadlocks possible for multiple seats
Unique index on (show\_id, seat\_id) in bookings
Last line of defence enforced by the store
Reports violation after the work; not a hold mechanism
In-memory hold (Redis SET NX with expiry)
Fast hold layer in front of the database
A second source of truth; must be reconciled with the database
blocks.caption: Concurrency control alternatives for a seat.

blocks.text: The following experiment runs the first alternatives on a real PostgreSQL 16 instance with 20 concurrent psql clients running 200 booking attempts against 2 hot seats. In strategies A, C and D the transaction sleeps 0.3 seconds between the check and the write to widen the race window to a size that the experiment can observe; the logic otherwise corresponds to production code. The scripts are shown first.

blocks.title: naive.sql (strategy A: read committed, no lock)

blocks.code:
WITH u AS (
  UPDATE seats SET status = 'SOLD', owner = :user
  WHERE seat_id = :seat AND status = 'AVAILABLE' RETURNING seat_id, owner)
INSERT INTO bookings(seat_id, user_id) SELECT seat_id, owner FROM u;
blocks.title: conditional.sql (strategy B: single conditional statement)

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Seat booking race on PostgreSQL 16: 200 attempts, 2 hot seats, 20 concurrent clients per strategy.
PSQL="psql -X -q -h /tmp/osw_y4/pg -p 22400 -U postgres -d seats"
reset() {
  $PSQL -c "TRUNCATE seats, bookings" \
        -c "INSERT INTO seats SELECT g, 'AVAILABLE', NULL FROM generate_series(1,2) g"
}
report() {
  $PSQL -At -c "SELECT '  seats SOLD=' || (SELECT count(*) FROM seats WHERE status='SOLD') ||
    '  booking rows=' || (SELECT count(*) FROM bookings) ||
    '  oversold seats=' || (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT seat_id FROM bookings
                          GROUP BY seat_id HAVING count(*)>1) s)"
}
run() {  # $1 = sql file
  seq 1 200 | xargs -P 20 -I{} sh -c \
    "$PSQL -v seat=\$(( ({}-1) % 2 + 1 )) -v user={} -f $1 2>/dev/null"
}
echo "A  check, then update (read committed, no lock)";   reset; run naive.sql;       report
echo "B  conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE'"; reset; run conditional.sql; report
echo "C  SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then check";              reset; run forupdate.sql;   report
echo "D  naive logic + UNIQUE(seat_id) on bookings";      reset
$PSQL -c "CREATE UNIQUE INDEX bookings_seat_uq ON bookings(seat_id)"; run naive.sql; report
$PSQL -c "DROP INDEX bookings_seat_uq"

blocks.text:
What to notice: in strategy A the clients of the first wave read AVAILABLE before any update committed, and each inserted a booking, so the two seats received 21 bookings in this run. The count varies between runs (20 in an earlier run) because it depends on timing and on the concurrency width of the experiment; the zero for strategies B, C and D does not vary. Strategy B needs no explicit lock: the database serialises the two updates on the same row, and the second one re-evaluates the predicate, finds status SOLD and updates zero rows. Strategy C serialises through the row lock at the price of holding it for the whole transaction; with multiple seats per hold, locks must be taken in a consistent order (sorted by seat\_id) to avoid deadlock. Strategy D shows the value of a constraint as a final safeguard: the naive logic still ran, but the unique index rejected the duplicate inserts. Decision: the conditional update (strategy B) as the primary mechanism, with the primary key and a unique booking index as safeguards. A Redis hold layer is added only if measurements show the database cannot absorb the hold rate; it adds a second source of truth that needs reconciliation.

#### Hold expiry and the payment race

A hold must expire without relying on a background job being timely. Storing `hold_expires_at` and treating `HELD` with an elapsed expiry as available (lazy expiry) makes the system correct at any moment; the expiry worker only tidies the seat-map cache and counters. The remaining problem is the time between payment submission and the gateway answer, which can exceed the hold. The checkout step therefore extends the hold by a grace period, and the confirmation step re-checks ownership and expiry. The program below models these rules with a virtual clock.

blocks.title: SeatHolds.java

blocks.code:
$ java SeatHolds.java
t=   0s  alice holds A1: true
t=   0s  bob tries A1: false (held by alice)
t= 590s  alice starts payment: true, hold now ends at t=890
t= 700s  bob tries A1 during payment: false
t= 880s  gateway answers, confirm(alice): true
t=1000s  carol holds B7: true
t=1700s  carol's payment succeeds at t=1700, hold ended at t=1600: false -> refund required
t=1700s  dave holds B7 (expired hold is reusable): true
t=1700s  A1 -> SOLD owner=alice
t=1700s  B7 -> HELD owner=dave
blocks.title: Run (JDK 21, deterministic: virtual clock)

blocks.text:
What to notice: Bob cannot take A1 while Alice is paying, because checkout moved it to PAYMENT\_PENDING with a later expiry; Alice's confirmation at t=880 succeeds inside the grace period. Carol's payment succeeds at t=1700 after her hold ended at t=1600; the confirmation returns false and the seat has been given to Dave, so the payment service must refund Carol. This is not an error path to be avoided but one that the design must handle explicitly, because gateway latency is outside the system's control.

#### Admission control for a flash sale

rows: Add instances behind the load balancer
The contention is on the same rows; more instances increase conflicts, not throughput
Rate limit per user and IP
Limits abuse; does not shape the aggregate rate
Users receive a random or ordered position and are admitted at a fixed rate with a signed token
Bounds the arrival rate at the inventory; fair
The system selects the best available seats for the party
Spreads conflicts; fewer clients compete for a given seat
blocks.caption: Handling a sale-opening burst.

blocks.text: The decisive point is that the bottleneck is logical contention on a small set of rows, not CPU. A waiting room converts 50,000 requests per second into 1,500 (500 admitted users per second at 3 requests each), at the price of a wait of up to 33 minutes for the last user in the assumed event. Admission order is randomised among users who arrived in the first minutes, because strict first-come ordering rewards bots with the fastest connections. Seat selection by the system ("best available") is an effective complement because it avoids a crowd of users all clicking the same front-row seats.

blocks.text:
### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Overselling under concurrency

**Scenario.** Two users select the last seat in the same second. **Symptoms.** Two confirmation emails for one seat; the venue reports a duplicate at the door. **Diagnosis.** Two booking rows reference the same (show\_id, seat\_id); the application log shows both transactions reading AVAILABLE. **Root cause.** A read-then-write sequence without a conditional update, lock or constraint. **Fix.** Conditional update with row-count verification; a unique index on booked seats as a safeguard; refund and apology for the affected customer. **Prevention.** A concurrency test that fires parallel requests at the same seat (as in the experiment above) in the continuous integration pipeline.

#### Abandoned holds block inventory

**Scenario.** Users select seats and close the browser. **Symptoms.** A show appears sold out while many seats are held; seats reappear only after 10 minutes. **Diagnosis.** The count of HELD seats with future expiry is high and the conversion rate is low; the seat map and the table differ if the cache is stale. **Root cause.** A fixed hold time is applied equally to genuine buyers and to idle sessions. **Fix.** Lazy expiry in the update predicate, a shorter hold at the start of the checkout steps (for example 5 minutes, refreshed on activity), explicit release on page exit, and a cap on seats held per user. **Prevention.** Track hold conversion by show and adapt the hold duration; alert on the held fraction of inventory.

#### Payment succeeds after the hold expired

**Scenario.** The gateway answers 40 seconds late; the seat was resold. **Symptoms.** A charged customer without a ticket. **Diagnosis.** A payment with status SUCCESS and no booking; the confirmation attempt returned false. **Root** **cause.** Time between submission and confirmation exceeded the hold. **Fix.** Extend the hold at checkout; on a failed confirmation refund automatically and notify the user; run a reconciliation job comparing successful payments with bookings. **Prevention.** Use the hold identifier as the payment idempotency key so retries cannot double charge, and monitor the late-confirmation rate.

#### Hot shard on a popular show

**Scenario.** All seats of one blockbuster show reside on one shard, which receives most of the sale traffic. **Symptoms.** The shard's CPU and lock wait times rise; other shows on the shard are slow. **Diagnosis.** Lock waits concentrate on one show\_id; per-shard QPS is skewed. **Root cause.** The partition key (show\_id) concentrates the contention by design, to keep a hold transaction on one shard. **Fix.** Admission control; move the show to a dedicated shard; serve the seat map from a read model; take holds in batches in one statement. **Prevention.** Provision dedicated capacity for announced high-demand sales, and rehearse with synthetic load.

#### Deadlock on multi-seat holds

**Scenario.** User X holds seats A1 and A2 while user Y requests A2 and A1. **Symptoms.** Occasional deadlock errors and aborted transactions. **Diagnosis.** The database log reports a deadlock between two transactions locking the same two rows in opposite order. **Root cause.** Row locks acquired in request order. **Fix.** Update seats in a single statement or order the seat identifiers before locking; retry the aborted transaction. **Prevention.** A coding rule: any multi-row write acquires rows in a canonical order.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- Strict consistency of inventory limits the write throughput per show to the capacity of one shard; this is acceptable because the inventory is small, and it is protected by admission control.
- A longer hold improves the payment success rate and increases the fraction of inventory that is unavailable to others; the right value is determined by measuring conversion.
- Showing "N seats left" requires either an exact counter (a contention point) or an approximate cached count; most products use the latter.
- Extension: general admission tickets (no seat identity) are a counter per section; the conditional update becomes `UPDATE ... SET remaining = remaining - n WHERE remaining >= n`.
- Extension: waitlists and resale subscribe to release events from the expiry worker.

### Questions to expect

#### How is double booking prevented?

By making ownership transfer a single conditional write on the seat row and verifying that exactly one row changed, with a unique constraint as a safeguard. The check and the write must not be separate steps.

#### Why not a distributed lock?

A distributed lock adds a service and failure modes (lease expiry, clock issues) for a problem that a single-row conditional update in the inventory database already solves atomically.

#### How does the seat map stay current?

It is a cache refreshed on every inventory change (or every second or two) and pushed to open clients over server-sent events or polling. Its staleness never affects correctness because the hold step validates against the table.

#### What if the booking service crashes after the payment succeeded?

The payment webhook is retried by the gateway and is idempotent. A reconciliation job compares successful payments without a booking and either completes the booking (if the hold is valid) or refunds.

#### How is the flash sale handled?

By a waiting room that admits users at a rate the database sustains, randomised ordering within an arrival window, per-user limits, and seat allocation by the system.

#### How are bots and scalpers limited?

Per-account and per-device purchase limits, rate limiting, proof-of-work or challenge in the waiting room, and verified accounts. None is fully effective; the design combines several layers.

#### Why is the booking separate from the payment?

The payment depends on an external system with unbounded latency. The hold decouples the scarce resource (seats) from that latency, and the idempotency key and reconciliation make the two-step process safe to retry.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Seat ownership is decided by a conditional update of one row, verified by its row count; a check followed by a write is a race.
- Holds carry an expiry timestamp and are treated as available after it, so correctness does not depend on a background job.
- Extend the hold at checkout and refund automatically when a payment succeeds after the seat has been resold.
- A waiting room turns an unbounded burst into a bounded, fair arrival rate; scaling out does not remove row contention.
- Keep constraints as a last safeguard and test concurrency explicitly with parallel requests.

An e-commerce platform has a read path that is large, cacheable and tolerant of staleness (catalog, search, product pages) and a write path that is small, transactional and intolerant of error (cart conversion, stock, order, payment). This chapter concentrates on the write path from cart to confirmed order. The distinguishing difficulty is that one business transaction spans several services with separate databases (orders, inventory, payments), so no single database transaction can protect it. The central decisions are how inventory is reserved, how the multi-service checkout is coordinated and made recoverable (the saga pattern), and how retries are made safe through idempotency.

### Requirements and scope

#### Functional requirements

- Users browse and search products, maintain a cart (also as guests), and check out.
- Checkout validates the cart, reserves stock, authorises payment, and creates an order.
- Users view order status and may cancel before shipment; cancellation releases stock and refunds the payment.
- Inventory is tracked per SKU and warehouse, with reservations that expire.

#### Non-functional requirements

- Never sell stock that does not exist (no overselling), never charge a customer twice for one order.
- Catalog read p99 below 100 ms; checkout API p99 below 1 second excluding the external payment call.
- The system tolerates the failure of any single service without losing or duplicating orders; every order reaches a terminal state.
- Availability above 99.95 percent for browsing and cart; checkout may reject new orders during a payment outage.

#### Out of scope

Search ranking, recommendations, tax and shipping rate computation, warehouse operations, marketplace seller settlement, and returns logistics. Fulfilment is represented as a consumer of order events.

#### Assumptions

All volumes are assumed: 50 million DAU, 4 product views per user per day, 100 million cart operations per day, 2 million orders per day with 3 items each, 50 million SKUs, a sale-event peak factor of 10 for reads and 20 for orders.

### Capacity estimation

rows: 23 orders per s x 6 events per order
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate (inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
The write path is small in absolute terms (463 orders per second at the peak), which a sharded relational store handles comfortably. Contention, not volume, is the problem: a promotion on one SKU concentrates the entire reservation load of the sale on one stock row. The read path, at 23,150 requests per second, is served almost entirely by caches and a CDN.

### API design

rows: Body: qty. Response: cart with prices and availability hints
Header Idempotency-Key. Body: cart\_id, cart\_version, address, payment method. Response 202: order\_id, state
Starts the saga; the client polls or subscribes
Response: state, items, payment status, tracking
blocks.caption: Cart, checkout and order API.

blocks.text:
The checkout key is derived by the client for each purchase attempt (for example a UUID generated when the checkout screen opens). It is stored in a unique column of the orders table, so a retried POST returns the existing order. The `cart_version` field makes the request fail with 409 if the cart changed after the user reviewed the total, which prevents a price or quantity mismatch between what was shown and what is charged. Per the Stripe API documentation on idempotent requests, a payment provider accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header with a key of up to 255 characters, returns the saved response for a repeated key, and rejects the same key with different parameters; keys may be pruned after at least 24 hours. The payment service of this design forwards the order identifier as that key.

blocks.text:
The order and its outbox rows share a database, so that one local transaction updates the state and records the event to be published (the transactional outbox pattern). A relay publishes unpublished outbox rows to the event bus and marks them; consumers must therefore tolerate duplicates. The stock table holds `on_hand` and `reserved` per (SKU, bucket); the available quantity is `on_hand - reserved`. The cart is a document keyed by user (or by a guest token) with a time to live; it is a convenience record, not a source of truth, and prices in it are re-evaluated at checkout.

### High-level architecture

blocks.text:
#### Checkout flow

1. The cart service sends the cart to the order service. The order service validates prices against the catalog, creates the order in state PENDING with the idempotency key, and commits the order and the outbox row in one transaction.
2. The relay publishes a `ReserveStock` command. The inventory service executes a conditional update per item, records a reservation with an expiry, and replies `StockReserved` or `OutOfStock`.
3. On `StockReserved`, the order service issues `AuthorizePayment` with the order id as idempotency key. The payment service calls the gateway and replies `PaymentAuthorized` or `PaymentDeclined`.
4. On success the order moves to CONFIRMED and fulfilment is notified. On `OutOfStock` or `PaymentDeclined` the order service runs the compensations for steps already completed (release the reservation) and the order becomes CANCELLED.
5. Payment is captured when the shipment is created, not at authorisation, so a cancellation before shipment only voids an authorisation.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Inventory accounting and hot SKUs

Stock is reserved at checkout, not when an item enters the cart. Reserving at add-to-cart holds stock for many users who never buy; reserving at payment completion allows a customer to pay for stock that is no longer there. The reservation is a single conditional statement:

blocks.title: Reserve stock

blocks.text: A reservation row with `expires_at` records the claim; a sweeper decrements `reserved` for expired reservations, and shipment converts the reservation into a decrement of `on_hand`. The row-level atomicity of the conditional update prevents overselling for the same reason as in the ticket booking design. When one SKU receives a large share of the traffic, the row lock held by each reservation transaction serialises them. Splitting the stock of a SKU into N bucket rows lets reservations proceed in parallel; a request selects a bucket at random and, on a zero-row result, tries another bucket before reporting out of stock. The experiment below uses pgbench with 20 clients against one hot SKU; every transaction holds its row lock for about 2 ms (modelling other work performed inside the transaction), with 1, 4 and 16 buckets.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Hot SKU: one stock row versus N buckets (PostgreSQL 16, pgbench, 20 clients, 5 s)
export PGOPTIONS="-c client_min_messages=warning"
export PGHOST=/tmp/osw_y4/pg PGPORT=22400 PGUSER=postgres
psql -X -q -d postgres -c "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS shop" -c "CREATE DATABASE shop"
cat > /tmp/osw_y4/e/reserve.sql <<'SQL'
\set b random(1, :nb)
BEGIN;
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 1 AND bucket = :b AND qty >= 1;
SELECT pg_sleep(0.002);
END;
SQL
for nb in 1 4 16; do
  psql -X -q -d shop -c "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stock" \
       -c "CREATE TABLE stock(sku int, bucket int, qty bigint, PRIMARY KEY (sku, bucket))" \
       -c "INSERT INTO stock SELECT 1, b, 1000000 / $nb FROM generate_series(1, $nb) b"
  echo "buckets=$nb"
  pgbench -n -c 20 -j 2 -T 5 -D nb=$nb -f /tmp/osw_y4/e/reserve.sql shop \
    | grep -E "tps|latency average"
  psql -X -At -d shop \
       -c "SELECT '  stock left=' || sum(qty) || ' min bucket=' || min(qty) FROM stock"
done

What to notice: with one row, throughput is bounded by the lock hold time (about 305 transactions per second at an average latency of 66 ms); with 16 buckets the same 20 clients achieve about 10 times the throughput (3,175 per second) at 6 ms; the figures vary by run. The remaining stock is consistent with the number of transactions executed and no bucket went negative. The cost of buckets is that the "available" figure is a sum over rows and that the last units of stock may be stranded in other buckets when one bucket is empty, which the retry across buckets mitigates.

#### Coordinating the checkout: saga

A distributed transaction across the order, inventory and payment databases (two-phase commit) would block resources during a slow payment call and is unavailable across most payment providers. The saga pattern replaces it with a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action.

Spread across services; harder to reason about
Simple two or three step reactions
blocks.caption: Saga coordination styles.

blocks.text: Decision: orchestration for checkout, because the process has ordered steps, timeouts and compensations that must be visible and testable in one place. The orchestrator persists its state in the order row, so after a crash it resumes from the recorded state; a timer finds orders stuck in an intermediate state longer than a limit and re-drives or cancels them. Every step must be idempotent because messages are delivered at least once and the orchestrator retries. The program below implements the orchestration with in-memory services and injected failures: a normal order, a declined card (with compensation), a lost payment reply followed by a retry with the same idempotency key, and exhausted stock.

blocks.title: CheckoutSaga.java

blocks.code:
$ java CheckoutSaga.java
1. normal order
  order o1 PENDING -> inventory reserved -> payment authorized
  result: CONFIRMED, stock={sku-1=1}
2. card declined
  order o2 PENDING -> inventory reserved -> compensation: inventory released
  result: CANCELLED (DECLINED), stock={sku-1=1}
3. first payment reply lost, orchestrator retries with the same key
  order o3 PENDING -> inventory reserved -> payment try 1 failed: timeout -> payment authorized
  result: CONFIRMED, stock={sku-1=0}, total authorizations=2 (o1 and o3)
4. stock exhausted
  result: CANCELLED (out of stock), stock={sku-1=0}
blocks.title: Run (JDK 21, deterministic)

blocks.text:
What to notice: in scenario 2 the reservation made in the first step is released by the compensation, so the stock returns to 1; in scenario 3 the payment was performed on the first call and the reply was lost, yet the retry with the same key returned the stored result, so only one authorisation exists for the order (two in total, for o1 and o3). Without the idempotency key the retry would have charged the customer twice. A real orchestrator adds persistence of its state, backoff between attempts, and a cap on attempts after which the order is cancelled and an operator alert is raised.

#### Idempotency and consistency of prices

Idempotency exists at three levels: the checkout key (one order per purchase attempt), the reservation key (the order id: a repeated `ReserveStock` returns the existing reservation) and the payment key (the order id). Prices are snapshotted into `order_items` at checkout; the catalog cache may be a few seconds stale, so the checkout step re-reads authoritative prices and rejects the request with 409 if the total differs from the one the user confirmed.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Overselling during a promotion

**Scenario.** A discounted item with 1,000 units receives 20,000 checkout attempts in one minute. **Symptoms.** Orders confirmed beyond stock, followed by cancellations and apologies; or the opposite, latency collapse on the stock row. **Diagnosis.** The sum of confirmed quantities exceeds the initial stock; lock wait time on one stock row dominates the database. **Root cause.** A read-check-write sequence for stock, or a single contended row for a hot SKU. **Fix.** The conditional update shown above and stock buckets for hot SKUs; reject early at the edge when a cached counter shows zero stock (a hint, never the decision). **Prevention.** Declare promotions in advance so that hot SKUs are pre-split into buckets, and load test with the expected concurrency.

#### Double charge on retry

**Scenario.** The payment gateway answers slowly; the order service times out and retries. **Symptoms.** The customer sees two charges; support receives complaints. **Diagnosis.** Two gateway transactions with different keys, or no key, for one order. **Root cause.** A retry that creates a new operation instead of repeating the same one. **Fix.** A deterministic idempotency key (order id) on every call; check the gateway for the transaction by key before retrying after an ambiguous failure; a reconciliation job that compares captures with orders daily. **Prevention.** Contract tests that inject a lost reply and assert a single charge.

#### Stuck saga

**Scenario.** The order service crashes between sending `AuthorizePayment` and receiving the reply. **Symptoms.** Orders remain in STOCK\_RESERVED; stock is reserved without an order progressing. **Diagnosis.** Orders in an intermediate state older than the timeout; reservations nearing their expiry. **Root cause.** The orchestrator's progress lived only in memory or the reply was lost. **Fix.** Persisted state and a recovery timer that re-sends the command (safe because it is idempotent) or cancels the order after a limit, releasing the reservation. **Prevention.** Alert on the age of the oldest non-terminal order, and test crash points between every pair of steps.

#### Duplicate or lost events from the outbox

**Scenario.** The relay publishes an event and crashes before marking it published. **Symptoms.** A consumer receives the same event twice (for example, two fulfilment tasks for one order). **Diagnosis.** Duplicate message ids in the consumer log. **Root cause.** At-least-once publication; the alternative of publishing before committing could lose events. **Fix.** Consumers deduplicate by event id (a processed-events table or a unique key on the effect); the outbox guarantees that no event is lost. **Prevention.** Design every consumer as idempotent and test it with duplicated delivery.

#### Phantom reservations

**Scenario.** Many checkouts are abandoned after the reservation, for example when users leave the payment page. **Symptoms.** Products appear out of stock while units sit in reservations. **Diagnosis.** The reserved quantity is high relative to confirmed orders; reservation age distribution shows many near the expiry. **Root cause.** Reservations that are released only at expiry. **Fix.** A short reservation time (for example 10 minutes), release on explicit cancel or payment failure, and a sweeper that runs frequently. **Prevention.** Monitor the ratio of reservations to confirmed orders per SKU.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- Reserving at checkout minimises phantom stock; some retailers instead oversell slightly and handle shortages by back-ordering, trading customer experience for conversion.
- Orchestration centralises the process and adds a component to keep available; choreography has no such component and is harder to understand as the number of steps grows.
- Authorise then capture reduces refunds on cancellation but requires capturing within the authorisation validity window.
- Extension: multi-warehouse allocation chooses the warehouse by distance and stock; reservations then name the warehouse.
- Extension: pre-orders and back-orders add a state between STOCK\_RESERVED and CONFIRMED.

### Questions to expect

#### Why not a distributed transaction (two-phase commit) across services?

It blocks resources for the duration of the slowest participant, the payment gateway does not take part in such protocols, and a coordinator failure leaves participants in doubt. A saga keeps each transaction local and uses compensation.

#### What is the transactional outbox and why is it needed?

It writes the event to a table in the same database transaction as the state change, and a relay publishes it afterwards. This avoids the dual-write problem: updating the database and the message broker cannot be made atomic, and one of them could succeed alone.

#### How is an idempotency key implemented?

A unique column (or table) stores the key with the result; the first request inserts the key and executes, a repeated request finds the key and returns the stored result, and a request with the same key and different parameters is rejected.

#### How is overselling prevented for a hot item?

By a conditional stock update, bucketed stock rows to avoid a single contended row, an edge hint to reject obviously sold-out requests, and, for extreme events, a waiting room as in the ticket booking design.

#### What happens if the payment succeeds but the order service fails to record it?

The payment service retains the authorisation keyed by the order id. On recovery the order service re-sends the command, receives the stored result, and continues; the reconciliation job detects authorisations without orders.

#### How is the cart kept when a guest logs in?

The guest cart (keyed by a token) is merged into the user's cart at login, summing quantities and keeping the most recent price evaluation; the guest document is then deleted.

#### How would cancellation after shipment work?

It becomes a return: a separate process creates a return authorisation, and the refund state follows delivery of the returned goods; stock is restored only after inspection.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A checkout spans several databases; replace the distributed transaction with an orchestrated saga of local transactions and compensations.
- Reserve stock at checkout with a conditional update; split a hot SKU into buckets, which raised throughput from 305 to 3,175 transactions per second in the experiment.
- Make every step idempotent: checkout key, reservation keyed by order id, payment keyed by order id.
- Use a transactional outbox so that state changes and events cannot diverge, and make consumers tolerate duplicates.
- Persist the saga state, time out intermediate states, and reconcile payments with orders.

Search autocomplete (typeahead) suggests completions for the text a user has typed so far, updating after every keystroke. It is a read-dominated service with extremely strict latency (the suggestions must appear before the next keystroke, which bounds the server time to a few tens of milliseconds) and a data set that is derived from the query history of all users. The design therefore separates an offline pipeline that computes popular completions from an online service that only performs a lookup. The central decisions are the data structure that answers prefix queries in time independent of the data size, the caching strategy that absorbs most of the traffic, and the update pipeline that keeps suggestions fresh and safe.

### Requirements and scope

#### Functional requirements

- Given a prefix, return the top 5 completions ranked by popularity.
- Suggestions reflect recent search behaviour: a newly trending query appears within minutes.
- Inappropriate or blocked terms never appear.
- Suggestions are specific to a locale (language and region).

#### Non-functional requirements

- Server latency p99 below 20 ms; end-to-end below 100 ms including the network.
- Peak load of several hundred thousand requests per second; availability above 99.99 percent (a missing suggestion degrades but does not break search).
- Suggestions may be slightly stale; they must never be offensive or illegal (a safety property, stricter than the freshness property).

#### Out of scope

Spelling correction and fuzzy matching, personalisation from the user's own history, semantic (embedding-based) suggestions, and search result ranking. Personalisation is discussed as an extension.

#### Assumptions

All volumes are assumed: 500 million DAU, 6 searches per user per day, 5 autocomplete requests per search (after client-side debouncing), peak factor 2, 100 million distinct queries retained after removing rare ones, an average query length of 25 characters.

### Capacity estimation

rows: Requests reaching the service (80 percent edge hit)
Service instances (10,000 per s each, assumed)
100e6 queries x about 3 nodes per query (shared prefixes)
300e6 nodes x 64 B (node plus 5 query ids)
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate (inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
Two results shape the design. The trie of about 19 GB fits in the memory of a single server, so the data does not need to be sharded for capacity: every replica holds the whole structure and any replica can answer any request, which gives simple load balancing and fault tolerance. And the request rate is dominated by a small set of very short prefixes, which makes caching extremely effective, as the following section shows.

### API design

rows: Query: q (prefix), limit (default 5), locale. Response: q, suggestions\[\], snapshot\_version
Body: query text, locale, ts. Response 202
Called by the search service when a search is executed, not by the typeahead
Takes effect at serving time without a rebuild
blocks.caption: Suggestion API.

blocks.text:
The request is a GET with the prefix in the query string, so that CDN and browser caches can store the response keyed by URL. The client waits 150 ms after the last keystroke before sending (debouncing), cancels a request that is still in flight when the next key is pressed, and ignores a response whose prefix no longer matches the input box. These client rules reduce the request rate by a large factor and are part of the system's capacity plan.

### Data model

Counts are aggregated per window (hour or day) and locale from the query log. The query dictionary assigns a numeric identifier to each distinct query so that the trie stores five small identifiers per node instead of five strings. The snapshot is an immutable file with a header, a node table and a string table; because it is read-only and laid out contiguously, it can be loaded or memory mapped by many replicas, and publishing a new version is a file swap rather than an in-place update.

blocks.text:
#### Online request flow

1. The client sends `GET /v1/suggest?q=tre` to the edge cache. A hit returns immediately (about 80 percent of requests in the estimate).
2. On a miss the edge forwards to an autocomplete service replica, which walks the trie one character at a time to the node for the prefix and returns the stored top-5 list. The walk costs a number of steps equal to the prefix length.
3. The service applies the live blocklist to the five results and returns them with a cache header of 60 seconds.

blocks.text:
#### Offline pipeline flow

1. The search service writes each executed query to a log stream.
2. The aggregation job counts queries per window and locale, applies decay to older windows and removes queries below a minimum count and those that match the blocklist.
3. The trie builder computes, for every node, the top five queries below it and writes a versioned snapshot to storage. Replicas download and load the new snapshot, then switch to it atomically.

### Deep dive

#### Data structure for prefix lookup

rows: Compare the prefix with every query
O(N) per request; unusable at 100 million queries
Walk to the prefix node, traverse the subtree, rank
Subtree of a short prefix contains millions of entries
Trie with top-k at each node
Precomputed list of the best k completions per node
Memory for lists; a count change updates L nodes
Hash map from every prefix to its list
More entries than a trie; no sharing of structure
Operational dependency; less control over ranking
blocks.caption: Prefix lookup alternatives.

blocks.text:
Decision: a trie with the top-k list stored at each node. The lookup is O(L) where L is the prefix length (typically below 10) and does not depend on the number of queries. The price is memory for the lists (5 identifiers per node, counted in the estimate) and a more expensive update: a change in the count of one query must refresh the lists of all L ancestors.

#### Verifying the trie

The program below builds such a trie for 89,637 synthetic queries with skewed popularity, answers 2,000 random prefixes both from the trie and by scanning all queries, checks that the results are identical, compares the lookup times, and shows how an update for a trending query propagates up the path. The vocabulary is synthetic; the structure and the measurements of the algorithm are real.

blocks.text:
What to notice: zero mismatches in 2,000 checks against the brute-force ranking; a lookup in under 3 microseconds against about 2.7 milliseconds for the scan, a factor near 1,000 on this data set, growing with the data size because the scan is linear and the trie lookup is not. The update at the end shows the propagation: a query given a count of 1,000,000 becomes the first suggestion for its prefixes immediately, because the call refreshes the lists of every node on its path (O(L x k) work). The ranking breaks ties by query text, which makes results deterministic and cacheable.

#### Ranking, decay and freshness

Ranking by total historical count favours old queries. Production systems weight recent windows more strongly, for example with an exponential decay `score = sum(count_w x 0.5^(age_w / half_life))` over windows, which lets the score of a query that stopped being searched fall away. Freshness is obtained by several paths with different cost:

blocks.text:
A common arrangement is a daily full rebuild for stability, an hourly incremental snapshot, and a small trending list computed from 5-minute windows that is merged at serving time into the results of matching prefixes. The merge keeps the large trie stable and limits the volume of data that changes quickly.

blocks.text:
Because a suggestion response depends only on the prefix, locale and snapshot, it is cacheable by URL at the CDN, in the browser (a short max-age), and in the service. The weighted hit ratio of 80 percent in the estimate follows from the assumed distribution of prefix lengths; it must be measured in production, and the long-prefix tail is the part that cannot be cached effectively.

#### Safe publication of snapshots

A defective snapshot reaches every user at once, so publication follows a gated rollout.

blocks.text:
Validation checks that the size is within a tolerance of the previous snapshot (for example plus or minus 20 percent), that no blocklisted term is present, and that a set of golden prefixes returns the expected leaders. A snapshot that fails any check is never loaded.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Offensive or legally problematic suggestion

**Scenario.** A coordinated group searches for a defamatory phrase until it becomes a top suggestion for a person's name. **Symptoms.** User reports and press attention; the phrase appears for a specific prefix. **Diagnosis.** The phrase has a high count concentrated in a short period; it passed the pipeline because it was not on the blocklist. **Root cause.** Popularity is the only ranking signal and popularity can be manufactured. **Fix.** Add the phrase to the live blocklist, applied at serving time so that no rebuild is needed, and purge the cached responses for the affected prefixes at the CDN. **Prevention.** Detect bursts from few distinct users (count distinct users per query, not only total count), apply classifiers for abusive content in the pipeline, and keep a fast removal path with an owner on call.

#### Bad snapshot deployment

**Scenario.** A pipeline bug drops half of the queries; the new snapshot is published to all replicas. **Symptoms.** Suggestions for many prefixes are empty; click-through on suggestions falls. **Diagnosis.** The snapshot size and node count are far below the previous version; quality metrics fell at the time of the switch. **Root cause.** The publication had no validation or staged rollout. **Fix.** Roll back to the previous snapshot on the replicas, which retain it. **Prevention.** The validation gate and canary shown above, and an automatic rollback on a quality alarm.

#### Cache expiry stampede on a popular prefix

**Scenario.** The cached entry of a very popular prefix expires at one edge location at the same moment for thousands of clients. **Symptoms.** A burst of identical misses reaches the service; latency spikes periodically at intervals of the TTL. **Diagnosis.** Request logs show many identical URLs within a few milliseconds after each expiry. **Root cause.** Synchronised expiry with no request coalescing. **Fix.** Coalesce concurrent misses for one URL at the edge, serve stale content while revalidating, and add random jitter to the TTL. **Prevention.** Load test expiry at peak traffic; monitor the origin request rate per URL.

#### Keystroke storm from clients

**Scenario.** A client release removes the debounce. **Symptoms.** The request rate rises by a factor of two to four without any change in the number of users. **Diagnosis.** Requests per search in the logs jump after the release date; the requests carry prefixes of increasing length from the same device within milliseconds. **Root cause.** The capacity plan depends on client behaviour that is not under server control. **Fix.** Roll back the client; add a per-client rate limit at the edge as protection. **Prevention.** Record requests per search as a service level indicator and alert on it.

#### Memory pressure and pauses

**Scenario.** The trie is built from millions of small objects on the heap. **Symptoms.** Long garbage-collection pauses and a high p99 on the replicas after loading a new snapshot. **Diagnosis.** Garbage-collection logs show pauses proportional to the live heap size; latency spikes align with snapshot loads. **Root cause.** An object-per-node representation of a 19 GB structure. **Fix.** Represent the trie as flat arrays or a memory-mapped file and load a new snapshot into a separate region before switching a pointer. **Prevention.** Keep the serving structure off the managed heap or in primitive arrays, and measure pauses in the load test.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- Storing top-k per node trades memory and update cost for lookup speed; a smaller k reduces memory, a larger k allows client-side filtering and personalisation re-ranking.
- Frequent snapshots improve freshness and increase operational risk and load; the trending side list is the compromise.
- Personalisation merges the global suggestions with the user's recent queries on the client or in a small per-user store, without changing the global trie.
- Extension: typo tolerance requires a fuzzy matching layer (edit distance automata or n-gram index) in front of or beside the trie.
- Extension: very large vocabularies or many locales are sharded by locale first, then by prefix range with weights, because the first-letter distribution is skewed.

### Questions to expect

#### Why store the top-k at every node rather than computing it per request?

Computing it requires traversing the subtree of the prefix, which for a one-letter prefix holds a large fraction of all queries. Precomputing makes the lookup depend only on the prefix length.

#### How is the trie updated when counts change?

Not in place for the bulk of the data: a new snapshot is built from aggregated counts and swapped in. A small trending structure handles fast changes and is merged at serving time. In-place updates refresh the top-k lists on the path, as the demonstration program does.

#### How is the system kept fast for the first letter, which has the largest subtree?

Its answer is precomputed and cached; the edge hit ratio for one-character prefixes is the highest, so they rarely reach the service.

#### How are results filtered for safety?

At three points: the aggregation removes blocklisted terms, validation rejects a snapshot containing any, and the service applies the live blocklist at response time so that a removal takes effect in seconds.

#### How would the design handle many languages?

A separate trie per locale, because prefixes and popularity differ, and because a unicode-aware tokeniser or normalisation (case folding, accents) is needed per language. The locale is part of the cache key.

#### What is the failure mode when the service is down?

The search box works without suggestions. The edge continues to serve cached responses (stale if necessary), so the system degrades gracefully rather than failing.

#### How is the dictionary of queries bounded?

By a minimum count threshold, a maximum query length, removal of queries that look like personal data (long numbers, email-like strings), and decay so that old queries expire.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Autocomplete is a lookup service: all ranking is computed offline and stored as the top-k list at each trie node, giving O(prefix length) lookups.
- Short prefixes dominate traffic and cache extremely well; the edge cache and client debouncing carry most of the load.
- Publish immutable, versioned snapshots through a validated, staged rollout with fast rollback.
- Combine a stable daily trie with a small trending list for freshness, and apply the blocklist at serving time for safety.
- Represent the serving trie in flat arrays or a mapped file to avoid garbage-collection pauses.

sections.title: Design: File Storage and Sync (Dropbox, Google Drive)

blocks.text:
A file storage and synchronisation service keeps a user's files identical on several devices and in the cloud, and allows folders to be shared. The workload mixes two very different kinds of data: a small, strongly consistent metadata set (the tree of names, versions and permissions) and a very large, immutable blob set (the bytes of files). The design problems are efficient transfer of large files that change slightly, detection and propagation of changes to every device, correct behaviour when two devices change the same file, and keeping the storage bill bounded. The central decisions are the chunking strategy, the commit protocol that separates data from metadata, and the conflict policy.

### Requirements and scope

#### Functional requirements

- Upload, download, rename, move and delete files and folders; files up to 50 GB.
- Automatic synchronisation of a folder tree to multiple devices, with offline edits merged on reconnection.
- File version history (30 days or the last 100 revisions) and restore.
- Sharing of folders with other users with read or edit permissions.

#### Non-functional requirements

- Durability of file content of at least 99.999999999 percent (eleven nines); a committed file is never lost.
- A change on one device is visible on other online devices within about 5 seconds for small files.
- Bandwidth efficiency: a small edit in a large file transfers a small amount of data.
- Metadata operations are strongly consistent per namespace (a user's folder tree); content transfer is eventually complete.

#### Out of scope

Real-time co-editing of documents (operational transformation or CRDTs), content search and preview generation, end-to-end encryption, and malware scanning. These attach to the journal of changes described below.

#### Assumptions

All volumes are assumed: 100 million daily active users, 500 petabytes of logical user data, 5 file changes per active user per day, an average changed file of 2 MB of which 40 percent of the bytes are uploaded after delta detection, an average of 200 files per user, 2 devices per user with 30 percent online at the peak, and a peak factor of 3.

### Capacity estimation

rows: Chunk index at 4 MiB (40 B each)
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate (inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
The chunk index is the item that depends most strongly on a design parameter: with chunks of 4 MiB the index is 4.8 TB and shards comfortably; with chunks of 64 KiB it is 305 TB, a large database in its own right. Smaller chunks give better deduplication and smaller deltas, larger chunks give a cheaper index and fewer requests; the choice of an average of a few MiB (4 MiB is assumed here) is a typical compromise. The demonstration later in this chapter uses 64 KiB chunks only because the files in the test are 8 MiB.

### API design

rows: Body: namespace, path, base\_rev, size, chunk\_hashes\[\]. Response: needs\_upload\[\] or revision
Called twice per change: negotiation, then final
Body: chunk bytes (up to 8 MiB). Response 200
The server verifies that the hash matches the content
Query: namespace, cursor, limit. Response: entries\[\], new\_cursor
Query: namespace, cursor, timeout (30 s). Response: changed (bool)
Adds an entry to the ACL
blocks.caption: Metadata and block API.

blocks.text:
The two-step commit is the core protocol. The client sends the list of chunk hashes of the new version; the server answers with those it does not already hold; the client uploads only those and repeats the commit, which succeeds if every chunk exists and `base_rev` equals the file's current revision (an atomic compare-and-set). Chunk upload is idempotent by construction (the key is the content hash), so interrupted uploads resume by re-sending the missing chunks.

### Data model

blocks.text:
A namespace is the unit of consistency: a user's root folder or a shared folder. All files, revisions and journal entries of a namespace live on one shard, so a commit, a rename or a directory move is a single-shard transaction. The journal is an append-only sequence with a monotonic cursor per namespace; every device records the last cursor it applied, and "what changed" is "all entries after my cursor". A revision stores an ordered list of chunk hashes; it does not contain bytes. The chunk table maps a hash to a storage location and a reference count. Because the hash identifies the content, the same chunk uploaded by different files is stored once.

### High-level architecture

blocks.text:
#### Upload flow

1. The sync client detects a change (file system events), splits the file into chunks, computes the SHA-256 of each, and calls `commit` with the chunk list and the base revision.
2. The metadata service checks which chunk hashes exist in the chunk table and returns the missing ones.
3. The client uploads the missing chunks to the block service, which verifies each hash and writes to block storage.
4. The client repeats `commit`. The metadata service verifies the chunks, compares the base revision, creates the new revision, appends a journal entry and returns the revision number.

blocks.text:
#### Download and synchronisation flow

1. Each device keeps a long poll open per namespace with its last cursor. When the journal advances, the notifier answers the poll.
2. The device calls `changes` with its cursor, receives the entries (file, revision, chunk hashes), downloads the chunks it does not hold locally, assembles the file, updates its local database and records the new cursor.

### Deep dive

#### Chunking strategy

rows: Any edit uploads the whole file; no deduplication inside files
An insertion shifts every later boundary: all later chunks change
Cut where a rolling hash of the last bytes matches a pattern
CPU cost of the rolling hash; variable chunk sizes
blocks.caption: Chunking alternatives.

blocks.text: The program below compares fixed 64 KiB chunks with content-defined chunking (a gear rolling hash with a boundary probability of 1 in 65,536 and chunk size limits of 16 KiB and 256 KiB) on an 8 MiB file under three edits. A chunk counts as "to upload" if its SHA-256 is not among the hashes of the previous version.

blocks.text:
What to notice: for the insertion, fixed chunking uploads 100 percent of the file and content-defined chunking uploads 0.6 percent, a reduction by a factor of about 150. For an overwrite in place (no shift) fixed chunking is slightly better (one chunk of 64 KiB against one content-defined chunk of 240 KiB, because content-defined chunks are variable and may be large). For an append both strategies upload about the appended 1 MiB. The result explains why synchronisation clients that must handle editors that rewrite files (insertions, reordered sections, compressed archives) use content-defined chunking, while workloads with in-place updates of fixed-size records can use fixed chunks.

#### Deduplication and storage cost

Chunks are addressed by the SHA-256 of their content, so identical chunks (the same file in two folders, a copy shared between users, unchanged parts of a new revision) are stored once. Cross-user deduplication has a privacy side effect: if the server answers "I already have this chunk" a user can test whether another user stored a specific file. A common countermeasure is to require proof that the client possesses the content (for example by hashing a server-supplied random challenge together with the chunk) before the server treats the chunk as present, or to limit deduplication to a single account or team. Durability is obtained by erasure coding of the stored chunks rather than by three full replicas. The estimate below shows the combined effect on 500 PB of logical data under assumed ratios.

blocks.text: #### Conflict resolution

rows: Reject the stale commit; client saves its version as a new file
No data loss; no merge logic
Requires format-specific logic; not possible for opaque files
blocks.caption: Conflict policies.

blocks.text: Decision: the conflicted-copy policy for generic files, enforced by the compare-and-set on `base_rev`. Editors with a document model can layer merge on top, using the journal as the transport.

blocks.text:
### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Orphaned chunks from interrupted uploads

**Scenario.** A client uploads 200 chunks of a large file and its laptop is closed before the final commit. **Symptoms.** Storage grows faster than the sum of live file sizes; chunk rows exist with a reference count of zero. **Diagnosis.** Chunks older than a day with no referencing revision; the gap between bytes stored and bytes referenced widens. **Root cause.** Chunks are written before the revision that references them, by design. **Fix.** A garbage collector that deletes chunks with zero references after a grace period (for example 24 hours), which also lets a resumed upload reuse the chunks. **Prevention.** Record the upload time on each chunk, and monitor the unreferenced fraction.

#### Race between garbage collection and a new commit

**Scenario.** The collector selects an unreferenced chunk for deletion at the moment a client commits a revision that references it by deduplication. **Symptoms.** A revision whose download fails with a missing chunk; data loss for one file. **Diagnosis.** A revision lists a hash that has no storage object. **Root cause.** Deletion decided on stale reference information. **Fix.** Delete only chunks that have been unreferenced for longer than the grace period, re-check the reference count in the same transaction that marks the chunk deleted, and make the commit increment the count before it returns success. **Prevention.** Verify chunk existence at commit time (already part of the protocol) and run an integrity scanner that compares revisions with storage.

#### Synchronisation loop between devices

**Scenario.** Two clients keep rewriting a file because an application changes its modification time or content when the file is opened. **Symptoms.** Constant sync traffic for one file; a long revision history; battery drain. **Diagnosis.** A rising revision count for one path, with revisions whose chunk lists are identical or alternate between two values. **Root** **cause.** Change detection by modification time rather than by content hash. **Fix.** Compare content hashes before committing; ignore a commit whose chunk list equals the latest revision; rate limit revisions per file. **Prevention.** Exclude temporary and lock files by pattern and alert on revision counts per path.

#### Initial synchronisation storm

**Scenario.** A new device or a team of 10,000 users begins synchronising several terabytes at once. **Symptoms.** Metadata service latency rises; block service bandwidth saturates; other users' sync slows. **Diagnosis.** A single namespace or a single tenant dominates request counts and bytes. **Root cause.** No per-tenant limits on listing and chunk transfer. **Fix.** Per-tenant and per-device rate limits, large batched `changes` pages, and prioritisation of small recent changes over bulk transfer. **Prevention.** Capacity tests with an onboarding scenario, and a scheduler that throttles bulk synchronisation during peak hours.

#### Hot shared namespace

**Scenario.** A shared folder with 100,000 members receives frequent changes. **Symptoms.** Journal appends and long-poll wake-ups on one shard saturate it; notifications lag. **Diagnosis.** One namespace id dominates both write rate and notification fan-out. **Root cause.** A namespace is a single consistency domain, so one shard serves all its traffic. **Fix.** Coalesce notifications (a poll response says "changed" once per interval, not once per change), batch journal reads, and cache recent journal pages. **Prevention.** Limit the membership of editable namespaces and treat very large shares as read-only publication.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- Chunk size trades index size and request count against deduplication and delta size; the choice of about 4 MiB targets the former, content-defined boundaries recover much of the latter.
- Strong consistency per namespace limits the write rate of one shared folder to the capacity of one shard; this is acceptable for the intended workload and enforced by limits.
- Client-side chunking and hashing costs CPU and battery on the device but moves the work off the servers and enables deduplication before upload.
- Extension: end-to-end encryption removes cross-user deduplication and server-side preview or search, because the server cannot see content.
- Extension: LAN synchronisation lets devices on the same network exchange chunks directly, using the chunk hash as the identifier.

### Questions to expect

#### Why separate chunk upload from the metadata commit?

Chunks are large, idempotent and addressed by content, so they can be uploaded in parallel, resumed and deduplicated without coordination. The commit is small and needs strong consistency. Separating them keeps the consistent component light and makes interrupted uploads harmless.

#### How does a device know what changed?

It stores the cursor of the last journal entry it applied and asks for the entries after it. A notification only triggers the request; losing a notification does not lose a change, because the next request with the same cursor returns it.

#### How are two simultaneous edits handled?

The commit carries the base revision; the server accepts it only if the file is still at that revision. The loser receives a conflict and stores its version as a conflicted copy, so no data is lost.

#### How are large files uploaded reliably?

As a sequence of chunks, each verified by its hash. A failure repeats only the missing chunks; after a restart the client calls the negotiation step again and receives the list of chunks still needed.

#### How are deleted files and old versions removed?

A delete creates a journal entry and a tombstone revision. Chunks lose references as revisions expire from the version history, and the collector removes chunks that stay unreferenced beyond the grace period.

#### How would permissions be enforced for shared folders?

Each namespace carries an access control list. The gateway authorises every metadata request against it; chunk downloads are authorised through the revision that references them (or short-lived signed URLs), never by hash alone, since a hash must not act as a capability.

#### Why is the notification channel separate from the metadata API?

Millions of mostly idle connections have a different resource profile from request-response traffic, as in the chat design: they need many cheap connections, while the metadata service needs transactional capacity.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Split the system into immutable, content-addressed chunks and a small strongly consistent metadata store with a per-namespace journal.
- Commit in two steps (negotiate missing chunks, then compare-and-set on the base revision) so that interrupted uploads are harmless and conflicts are detected.
- Content-defined chunking made an insertion cost 0.6 percent of the file instead of 100 percent in the experiment; choose the average chunk size for index cost and delta size.
- Devices pull changes by cursor; notifications are hints and cannot lose changes.
- Keep both versions on conflict, delete chunks only after a grace period and a reference re-check, and use erasure coding and deduplication to bound storage.

A payment system moves money on behalf of its users: it charges a customer through an external payment service provider (PSP), records the resulting obligations, and may hold balances that users transfer among themselves (a wallet). The requirements differ from other designs in this part: the cost of an error is direct financial loss, so correctness, auditability and recoverability take priority over latency and even over availability in some paths. The system must produce the effect of each payment exactly once although every network call can fail, time out or be repeated. The central decisions are the idempotency design, the double-entry ledger as the record of truth, the handling of outcomes that are unknown, and reconciliation with the external world.

### Requirements and scope

#### Functional requirements

- A merchant creates a payment for an amount and currency; the customer pays with a card or another method held by the PSP (tokenised: this system never stores card numbers).
- Payments support authorisation, capture, void and (partial) refund.
- Users hold wallet balances, top them up, and transfer between wallets.
- Every movement of money is recorded in an auditable ledger; balances are queryable.
- A daily reconciliation compares internal records with the PSP's settlement report.

#### Non-functional requirements

- Exactly-once effect: no double charge, no lost payment, no negative wallet balance.
- Strong consistency of the ledger; durability with synchronous replication before a payment is acknowledged.
- Payment initiation availability above 99.99 percent; latency p99 below 2 seconds, dominated by the PSP.
- Full audit trail: every state change is attributable and no record is modified or deleted.

#### Out of scope

Card data handling and PCI DSS compliance (reduced by tokenisation and hosted payment fields, covered by reference in the security material), fraud scoring, foreign exchange, payouts to bank accounts, tax, and regulatory reporting.

#### Assumptions

All volumes are assumed: 10 million PSP payments per day, 20 million wallet transfers per day, a peak factor of 10 for payments and 5 for transfers, 4 ledger entries per payment and 2 per transfer, 200 bytes per ledger entry, idempotency keys retained for 7 days.

### Capacity estimation

blocks.caption: Capacity estimate (inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
The throughput is low by the standards of the other designs: a few thousand writes per second fit one sharded relational cluster with synchronous replication. The engineering effort therefore goes into correctness under failure rather than into scale. Storage is also modest and grows linearly, since ledger entries are never deleted.

### API design

rows: Header Idempotency-Key. Body: merchant\_id, amount\_minor, currency, payment\_method\_token. Response 201: payment\_id, state
Amount is an integer in minor units
Capture at most the authorised amount
Cumulative refunds cannot exceed the captured amount
Read from the primary for read-your-writes
Header Idempotency-Key. Body: to\_wallet, amount\_minor, currency. Response 201 or 422 (insufficient funds)
Signed event: event\_id, type, psp\_ref, status
blocks.caption: Payment and wallet API.

blocks.text:
Money is represented as integers in the smallest currency unit with an explicit currency code. Floating-point numbers are never used, because values such as 0.1 have no exact binary representation and rounding errors accumulate; fee splits that do not divide evenly are allocated by a defined rule (the remainder goes to a named account) so that the entries still sum to the total. Per the Stripe API documentation on idempotent requests, a key may be up to 255 characters, the first result for a key is stored and returned on retries (including error results), a retry with different parameters is rejected, and keys may be removed after at least 24 hours. This design adopts the same contract for its own API and forwards a derived key to the PSP.

blocks.text: The ledger is the source of truth for money inside the system. A ledger transaction groups two or more entries whose signed amounts sum to zero (debits negative, credits positive in this representation). Entries are only ever inserted. The balance of an account is the sum of its entries; a cached balance column may be kept for fast reads and for the overdraft check, but it is maintained in the same database transaction as the entries and can always be recomputed and verified from them. The payment row holds the business state; the ledger holds the financial consequences.

blocks.caption: The payment service coordinates the idempotency store, the PSP adapter and the ledger; the PSP reports outcomes asynchronously through webhooks and daily through the settlement file used by reconciliation.
blocks.alt: Webhook | receiver | webhook | Merchant app API gateway Payment service PSP adapter External PSP | checkout auth, rate limit state machine timeouts, retries and bank | key entries settlement | Idempotency Ledger service Ledger DB Reconciliation | store double entry append-only job

blocks.text:
#### Payment flow

1. The merchant calls `POST /v1/payments` with an Idempotency-Key. The gateway authenticates the caller; the payment service inserts the key into the idempotency store (a unique insert). If the key exists, the stored response is returned and processing ends.
2. The payment row is created in state CREATED and moved to PROCESSING in the same transaction that records the intent to call the PSP.
3. The PSP adapter calls the PSP with a key derived from the payment id, with a timeout and bounded retries.
4. On an answer, the payment service updates the state (AUTHORIZED or FAILED) with a compare-and-set on the version, writes the ledger transaction when money is committed (capture), stores the response under the idempotency key, and replies to the merchant.
5. If there is no answer, the state becomes UNKNOWN. A background resolver queries the PSP by key and, in parallel, the webhook receiver may deliver the outcome; whichever arrives first resolves the payment, and the second is recognised as a duplicate.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Idempotency

Retries come from every layer: mobile clients, load balancers, the service itself and the PSP. The effect of a request must occur once, whatever the number of deliveries. The protocol is:

1. The client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID created when the user confirms the payment) and sends it on every retry.
2. The server inserts (key, request hash) with a unique constraint before doing any work. The first insert wins and proceeds.
3. A later request with the same key and the same request hash returns the stored response, or 409 if the first request is still in progress. A later request with the same key and a different request hash is rejected with 422, because it indicates a client bug.
4. The result of the operation, including a failure that is final, is stored under the key in the same transaction as the state change, so that the stored result and the effect cannot diverge.

The key must also be carried to every external side effect. The PSP call uses a key derived from the payment id and attempt purpose, so that a retry after a timeout cannot create a second charge at the provider.

#### Double-entry ledger and concurrent transfers

Double-entry bookkeeping guarantees a global invariant: the sum of all ledger entries is zero, so money is neither created nor destroyed by a bug in a single code path. A wallet transfer debits one account and credits another in one database transaction. Two concurrency hazards follow: an overdraft (two concurrent transfers each see enough balance) and a deadlock (two transfers lock the same two accounts in opposite orders). The experiment below creates 4 accounts with 1,000 units each and runs 1,000 transfer attempts from 20 concurrent clients over 200 distinct idempotency keys (so most attempts are retries of an earlier key, and parameters are determined by the key). The `transfer_naive` function locks the source account, waits 2 ms (modelling other work), then locks the destination; `transfer_ordered` locks both rows in one statement ordered by account id.

blocks.title: ledger_setup.sql

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Double-entry transfers on PostgreSQL 16: 20 clients, 1,000 attempts, 200 idempotency keys
export PGOPTIONS="-c client_min_messages=warning -c deadlock_timeout=50ms"
export PGHOST=/tmp/osw_y4/pg PGPORT=22400 PGUSER=postgres
psql -X -q -d postgres -c "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS pay" -c "CREATE DATABASE pay"
for fn in transfer_naive transfer_ordered; do
  psql -X -q -d pay -f ledger_setup.sql
  cat > /tmp/osw_y4/p/t.sql <<SQL
\set k random(1, 200)
\set a (:k % 4) + 1
\set b ((:k / 4) % 4) + 1
\set amt (:k % 7) * 40 + 40
SELECT $fn(:k, :a, :b, :amt);
SQL
  echo "== $fn"
  pgbench -n -c 20 -j 2 -t 50 --failures-detailed -f /tmp/osw_y4/p/t.sql pay \
    | grep -E "failed transactions|deadlock"
  psql -X -At -d pay \
    -c "SELECT 'transfers: ' || count(*) || ' (ok ' || count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='OK')
        || ', rejected ' || count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='REJECTED') || ')' FROM transfers" \
    -c "SELECT 'ledger entries: ' || count(*) || '  sum of amounts: ' || coalesce(sum(amount),0)
        FROM ledger_entries" \
    -c "SELECT 'accounts total: ' || sum(balance) || '  min balance: ' || min(balance)
        FROM accounts" \
    -c "SELECT 'accounts disagreeing with ledger: ' || count(*) FROM accounts a
        WHERE a.balance <> 1000 + coalesce((SELECT sum(amount) FROM ledger_entries l
                                             WHERE l.account_id = a.account_id), 0)"
done

blocks.text:
What to notice: the invariants held in both runs, which is the point of using database transactions for the ledger: the sum of entries is zero, the account total is still 4,000, no balance went negative (the `CHECK` constraint and the explicit balance test), and the cached balances agree with the entries. The unordered variant paid for correctness with availability: 486 of 1,000 attempts were aborted as deadlock victims and had to be retried by the caller, which is safe only because of the idempotency key. Duplicate keys were absorbed by the unique insert into `transfers` (199 distinct keys in the ordered run, each executed once). The ordered variant yields identical financial results without aborts; the rule is to acquire row locks in a canonical order, here ascending account id.

#### Unknown outcomes and webhooks

A call to the PSP can end in three ways: success, a definitive failure, or no answer. The third must not be treated as failure (the customer may have been charged) or as success. The payment enters UNKNOWN; the resolver queries the PSP by the idempotency key until it obtains a definitive answer, and an unresolved payment after a limit is escalated to manual review. Webhooks provide the same information asynchronously. They can arrive late, twice or out of order, so the handler verifies the signature, deduplicates by event id, and applies a transition only if it is valid from the current state (a late AUTHORIZED event cannot move a CAPTURED payment backwards).

#### Reconciliation

The PSP's settlement report is the independent record of what money actually moved. A daily job matches each report row with a captured payment on provider reference, amount and currency and sorts the differences into classes.
